claim: Visual pigments can be spontaneously activated by internal thermal energy, generating noise that interferes with real-light detection.
source: Visual pigments can be spontaneously activated by internal thermal energy, generating noise that interferes with real-light detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baylor et al., 1980 in the Introduction section, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: A physicochemical theory successfully predicts the rate of spontaneous activity of representative rod and cone pigments from their peak-absorption wavelength (λmax).
source: Recently, we developed a physicochemical theory that successfully predicts the rate of spontaneous activity of representative rod and cone pigments from their peak-absorption wavelength (λmax), with pigments having longer λmax being noisier.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Luo et al., 2011) and represents a primary finding of that work.

claim: Pigments having longer λmax are noisier.
source: Recently, we developed a physicochemical theory that successfully predicts the rate of spontaneous activity of representative rod and cone pigments from their peak-absorption wavelength (λmax), with pigments having longer λmax being noisier.
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by the physicochemical theory and experimental data from Luo et al., 2011.

claim: Cone pigments may generally be ~25 fold noisier than rod pigments of the same λmax.
source: Interestingly, cone pigments may generally be ~25 fold noisier than rod pigments of the same λmax, possibly ascribed to an 'open' chromophore-binding pocket in cone pigments defined by the capability of chromophore-exchange in darkness.
evidence: This is supported by measurements and theoretical analysis from Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The openness of cone pigments' chromophore-binding pocket is defined by the capability of chromophore-exchange in darkness.
source: Interestingly, cone pigments may generally be ~25 fold noisier than rod pigments of the same λmax, possibly ascribed to an 'open' chromophore-binding pocket in cone pigments defined by the capability of chromophore-exchange in darkness.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on the observed property of chromophore-exchange in cone pigments.

claim: The λmax-dependence of pigment noise can be extended to E122Q-rhodopsin mutant pigment.
source: Here, we show in mice that the λmax-dependence of pigment noise could be extended even to a mutant pigment, E122Q-rhodopsin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin shows some cone-pigment-like characteristics.
source: Moreover, although E122Q-rhodopsin shows some cone-pigment-like characteristics, its noise remained quantitatively predictable by the 'non-open' nature of its chromophore-binding pocket as in wild-type rhodopsin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imai et al., 2007 and by experimental observations in the current study.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin noise is quantitatively predictable by the 'non-open' nature of its chromophore-binding pocket as in wild-type rhodopsin.
source: Moreover, although E122Q-rhodopsin shows some cone-pigment-like characteristics, its noise remained quantitatively predictable by the 'non-open' nature of its chromophore-binding pocket as in wild-type rhodopsin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental measurements and theoretical predictions.

claim: The openness/closedness of the chromophore-binding pocket is potentially a useful indicator of whether a pigment is intended for detecting dim or bright light.
source: The openness/closedness of the chromophore-binding pocket is potentially a useful indicator of whether a pigment is intended for detecting dim or bright light.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Retinal rod and cone photoreceptors have similar phototransduction mechanisms.
source: Retinal rod and cone photoreceptors, although having similar phototransduction mechanisms, elaborate different morphological and molecular features for functioning in dim and bright light, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of vision science.

claim: Rod and cone photoreceptors elaborate different morphological and molecular features for functioning in dim and bright light, respectively.
source: Retinal rod and cone photoreceptors, although having similar phototransduction mechanisms, elaborate different morphological and molecular features for functioning in dim and bright light, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of vision science.

claim: Rod pigments have a low rate of spontaneous activation in darkness.
source: At the pigment level, rod pigments have a low rate of spontaneous activation in darkness (Baylor et al., 1980), thus offering a good signal-to-noise ratio for dim-light vision.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baylor et al., 1980.

claim: Low spontaneous activation rate in rod pigments offers a good signal-to-noise ratio for dim-light vision.
source: At the pigment level, rod pigments have a low rate of spontaneous activation in darkness (Baylor et al., 1980), thus offering a good signal-to-noise ratio for dim-light vision.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between noise and signal detection.

claim: Spontaneous activation originates from internal thermal energy of the pigment molecule.
source: Spontaneous activation originates from internal thermal energy of the pigment molecule, generating an electrical event indistinguishable from that triggered by an absorbed photon (Baylor et al., 1980), thus interfering with real-light detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baylor et al., 1980 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Spontaneous activation generates an electrical event indistinguishable from that triggered by an absorbed photon.
source: Spontaneous activation originates from internal thermal energy of the pigment molecule, generating an electrical event indistinguishable from that triggered by an absorbed photon (Baylor et al., 1980), thus interfering with real-light detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baylor et al., 1980.

claim: A pigment's spontaneous activity originates from thermal isomerization, with an energy barrier closely related to the pigment's λmax.
source: Recently, Luo et al. (2011) have developed a macroscopic physicochemical theory about pigment noise based on the notion that a pigment's spontaneous activity originates from thermal isomerization, with an energy barrier closely related to the pigment's λmax.
evidence: This is the theoretical foundation developed by Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The theory using multi-vibrational-mode statistical mechanics was able to explain quantitatively the λmax-dependence of pigment noise.
source: By using multi-vibrational-mode statistical mechanics (Ala-Laurila et al., 2004; Hinshelwood, 1940; St George, 1952), the theory was able to explain quantitatively the λmax-dependence of pigment noise, with the noise increasing by 107-fold from blue (short-wavelength-sensitive, or SWS) cone pigment to red (long-wavelength-sensitive, or LWS) cone pigment (Fu et al., 2008; Kefalov et al., 2003; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the theoretical framework and experimental data.

claim: Pigment noise increases by 107-fold from blue (SWS) cone pigment to red (LWS) cone pigment.
source: By using multi-vibrational-mode statistical mechanics (Ala-Laurila et al., 2004; Hinshelwood, 1940; St George, 1952), the theory was able to explain quantitatively the λmax-dependence of pigment noise, with the noise increasing by 107-fold from blue (short-wavelength-sensitive, or SWS) cone pigment to red (long-wavelength-sensitive, or LWS) cone pigment (Fu et al., 2008; Kefalov et al., 2003; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements cited from Fu et al., 2008; Kefalov et al., 2003; Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The theory clarifies that spontaneous pigment activity arises from canonical isomerization of the pigment's chromophore rather than from some different, unknown chemical reaction.
source: This theory clarifies the decades-long uncertainty about whether the spontaneous pigment activity arises from canonical isomerization of the pigment's chromophore (as in photoisomerization) or from some different, unknown chemical reaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical and experimental work cited.

claim: A cone pigment has a higher molecular frequency of attempting to cross the isomerization barrier compared to a rod pigment of the same λmax.
source: The simplest interpretation is that a cone pigment has a higher molecular frequency of attempting to cross the isomerization barrier (Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the theoretical framework from Luo et al., 2011.

claim: A number of cone pigments show observable dark chromophore-exchange without isomerization when exposed to another chromophore.
source: Concurrently, unlike rod pigment, a number of cone pigments show observable dark chromophore-exchange without isomerization when exposed to another chromophore (Kefalov et al., 2005; Matsumoto et al., 1975), suggesting a tendency of spontaneous dissociation between apo-cone-opsin and 11-cis-retinal by Schiff-base hydrolysis, in turn implicating the binding pocket being accessible – or 'open' – to external water.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kefalov et al., 2005 and Matsumoto et al., 1975.

claim: Dark chromophore-exchange in cone pigments suggests a tendency of spontaneous dissociation between apo-cone-opsin and 11-cis-retinal by Schiff-base hydrolysis.
source: Concurrently, unlike rod pigment, a number of cone pigments show observable dark chromophore-exchange without isomerization when exposed to another chromophore (Kefalov et al., 2005; Matsumoto et al., 1975), suggesting a tendency of spontaneous dissociation between apo-cone-opsin and 11-cis-retinal by Schiff-base hydrolysis, in turn implicating the binding pocket being accessible – or 'open' – to external water.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed chromophore-exchange behavior.

claim: Dark chromophore-exchange implicates the binding pocket being accessible – or 'open' – to external water.
source: Concurrently, unlike rod pigment, a number of cone pigments show observable dark chromophore-exchange without isomerization when exposed to another chromophore (Kefalov et al., 2005; Matsumoto et al., 1975), suggesting a tendency of spontaneous dissociation between apo-cone-opsin and 11-cis-retinal by Schiff-base hydrolysis, in turn implicating the binding pocket being accessible – or 'open' – to external water.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of Schiff-base hydrolysis requiring water access.

claim: The 'openness' of cone pigments' chromophore-binding pocket imposes less constraint on the chromophore's attempts to isomerize spontaneously, resulting in higher thermal noise compared to rod pigments for a given λmax.
source: It was hypothesized that this 'openness' of cone pigments' chromophore-binding pocket – defined by the property of dark chromophore-exchange – imposes less constraint on the chromophore's attempts to isomerize spontaneously, resulting in a higher thermal noise compared to rod pigments for a given λmax (Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The E122Q mutation in rhodopsin causes a blue-shift in λmax to ~480 nm from ~500 nm in wild-type rhodopsin.
source: This E122Q mutation causes a blue-shift in λmax to ~480 nm from ~500 nm in wild-type (WT) rhodopsin (Imai et al., 2007), substantial enough for validating the quantitative connection between pigment noise and λmax.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imai et al., 2007.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin has acquired some cone-pigment-like properties such as faster decays of the meta-II and meta-III states as well as a shift of the meta-I/meta-II equilibrium.
source: Equally interestingly, this mutant rhodopsin has acquired some cone-pigment-like properties such as faster decays of the meta-II and meta-III states as well as a shift of the meta-I/meta-II equilibrium (Imai et al., 2007), although retaining the indication of a closed chromophore-binding pocket as gleaned from in vitro experiments (Sakurai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imai et al., 2007.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin retains the indication of a closed chromophore-binding pocket as gleaned from in vitro experiments.
source: Equally interestingly, this mutant rhodopsin has acquired some cone-pigment-like properties such as faster decays of the meta-II and meta-III states as well as a shift of the meta-I/meta-II equilibrium (Imai et al., 2007), although retaining the indication of a closed chromophore-binding pocket as gleaned from in vitro experiments (Sakurai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sakurai et al., 2007.

claim: RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods have broadly similar morphology as RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods.
source: RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods had broadly similar morphology as RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression levels of the pigment and other phototransduction components are normal in RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- retinae based on Western blot analysis.
source: Expression levels of the pigment and other phototransduction components were also normal in mutant retinae based on Western blot analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The spontaneous-activation rate for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C is 0.015 ± 0.010 s−1 cell−1.
source: Collective data at 37.5°C gave 0.015 ± 0.010 s−1 cell−1 (mean ± SD, n = 12) for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods, and 0.0024 ± 0.0025 s−1 cell−1 (n = 20) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the current study.

claim: The spontaneous-activation rate for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C is 0.0024 ± 0.0025 s−1 cell−1.
source: Collective data at 37.5°C gave 0.015 ± 0.010 s−1 cell−1 (mean ± SD, n = 12) for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods, and 0.0024 ± 0.0025 s−1 cell−1 (n = 20) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the current study.

claim: The measurements from RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods matched previous estimates.
source: The measurements from RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods matched previous estimates (Burns et al., 2002; Fu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: The spontaneous events in RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods follow a Poisson distribution.
source: Indeed, the resulting probability histogram fits the Poisson distribution (red lines in Figure 1D), with the probability, p(u), of observing u events in each epoch being given by p(u)=wue−w/u!, where w is the average number of events per epoch.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fit shown in Figure 1D.

claim: From Poisson analysis, the thermal rate for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C is 0.0023 s−1 cell−1.
source: From altogether 118 epochs from 20 rods, we obtained the w value, giving a thermal rate of 0.0023 s−1 cell−1 for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C, very similar to the above measurement.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the current study using Poisson analysis.

claim: The spontaneous-activation rate from power spectrum analysis for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C is 0.0025 ± 0.005 s−1 cell−1.
source: From the scaling factor, we obtained a spontaneous-activation rate of 0.0025 ± 0.005 s−1 cell−1 (n = 11) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods at 37.5°C, very similar to that from the first method.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the current study using power spectrum analysis.

claim: A mouse rod contains 6.5 × 10^7 rhodopsin molecules.
source: For a total of 6.5 × 107 rhodopsin molecules in a mouse rod (Luo et al., 2011), the overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation from either method above was 3.69 × 10−11 s−1, ~6-fold lower than WT (2.31 × 10−10 s−1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation for E122Q-rhodopsin is 3.69 × 10−11 s−1.
source: For a total of 6.5 × 107 rhodopsin molecules in a mouse rod (Luo et al., 2011), the overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation from either method above was 3.69 × 10−11 s−1, ~6-fold lower than WT (2.31 × 10−10 s−1).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental measurements in the current study.

claim: The molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation for E122Q-rhodopsin is ~6-fold lower than wild-type rhodopsin.
source: For a total of 6.5 × 107 rhodopsin molecules in a mouse rod (Luo et al., 2011), the overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation from either method above was 3.69 × 10−11 s−1, ~6-fold lower than WT (2.31 × 10−10 s−1).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental measurements in the current study.

claim: The overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation for wild-type rhodopsin is 2.31 × 10−10 s−1.
source: For a total of 6.5 × 107 rhodopsin molecules in a mouse rod (Luo et al., 2011), the overall molecular rate constant of spontaneous activation from either method above was 3.69 × 10−11 s−1, ~6-fold lower than WT (2.31 × 10−10 s−1).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental measurements in the current study.

claim: The pre-exponential factor A is 7.19 × 10−6 s−1 for rod pigments with a 'closed' binding pocket.
source: The pre-exponential factor A, taken to represent the frequency at which a pigment molecule attempts to isomerize thermally, was found in previous work (Luo et al., 2011) to be 7.19 × 10−6 s−1 for rod pigments (with a 'closed' binding pocket) and 1.88 × 10−4 s−1 for cone pigments (with an 'open' binding pocket), a 26-fold difference.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The pre-exponential factor A is 1.88 × 10−4 s−1 for cone pigments with an 'open' binding pocket.
source: The pre-exponential factor A, taken to represent the frequency at which a pigment molecule attempts to isomerize thermally, was found in previous work (Luo et al., 2011) to be 7.19 × 10−6 s−1 for rod pigments (with a 'closed' binding pocket) and 1.88 × 10−4 s−1 for cone pigments (with an 'open' binding pocket), a 26-fold difference.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2011.

claim: There is a 26-fold difference in the pre-exponential factor A between rod and cone pigments.
source: The pre-exponential factor A, taken to represent the frequency at which a pigment molecule attempts to isomerize thermally, was found in previous work (Luo et al., 2011) to be 7.19 × 10−6 s−1 for rod pigments (with a 'closed' binding pocket) and 1.88 × 10−4 s−1 for cone pigments (with an 'open' binding pocket), a 26-fold difference.
evidence: This is calculated from the values reported in Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The λmax of E122Q-rhodopsin is 481 nm.
source: Inserting T = (37.5 + 273) oK = 310.5 oK, m = 45 [see (Luo et al., 2011)], and λmax = 481 nm for E122Q-rhodopsin (Figure 2A), we predict a molecular thermal-rate constant of 3.68 × 10−11 s−1 for a 'closed', and 9.63 × 10−10 s−1 for an 'open', binding pocket.
evidence: This is measured in the current study and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The predicted molecular thermal-rate constant for E122Q-rhodopsin with a 'closed' binding pocket is 3.68 × 10−11 s−1.
source: Inserting T = (37.5 + 273) oK = 310.5 oK, m = 45 [see (Luo et al., 2011)], and λmax = 481 nm for E122Q-rhodopsin (Figure 2A), we predict a molecular thermal-rate constant of 3.68 × 10−11 s−1 for a 'closed', and 9.63 × 10−10 s−1 for an 'open', binding pocket.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical equation using the measured λmax.

claim: The predicted molecular thermal-rate constant for E122Q-rhodopsin with an 'open' binding pocket is 9.63 × 10−10 s−1.
source: Inserting T = (37.5 + 273) oK = 310.5 oK, m = 45 [see (Luo et al., 2011)], and λmax = 481 nm for E122Q-rhodopsin (Figure 2A), we predict a molecular thermal-rate constant of 3.68 × 10−11 s−1 for a 'closed', and 9.63 × 10−10 s−1 for an 'open', binding pocket.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical equation using the measured λmax.

claim: The predicted rate for a 'closed' pocket matched the measurement very well for E122Q-rhodopsin.
source: Thus, the predicted rate for a 'closed' pocket matched the measurement very well.
evidence: This is a comparison between the predicted value (3.68 × 10−11 s−1) and the measured value (3.69 × 10−11 s−1).

claim: A biochemical method found a higher thermal rate constant of E122Q-rhodopsin over WT rhodopsin.
source: Recently, one of the authors here (Y.S.) has found biochemically a higher instead of lower thermal rate constant of E122Q-rhodopsin over WT rhodopsin (Yanagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yanagawa et al., 2015.

claim: The discrepancy between biochemical and electrophysiological measurements may arise from using detergent-solubilized samples in the biochemical method.
source: This discrepancy may arise from using detergent-solubilized samples in the biochemical method.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of the discrepancy.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin shows no dark chromophore-exchange when incubated with 9-cis-retinal for 3 hours.
source: No spectral shift was detected in the 9-cis-exposed rods, suggesting no dark chromophore-exchange, which is similar in behavior to RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/-rods (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: E122Q-rhodopsin shows no apparent chromophore-exchange even with 6 hr of dark incubation with 9-cis-retinal.
source: We found no apparent exchange even with 6 hr of dark incubation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After 99%-bleach, E122Q-rhodopsin shows spectral shift when incubated with 9-cis-retinal, indicating normal hydrolysis and formation of the Schiff-base.
source: As control, we delivered a 99%-bleach by 500 nm light to the rods prior to dark incubation with 9-cis. In this case, a spectral shift occurred in RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods as in RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods (Figure 2D), indicating normal hydrolysis and formation of the Schiff-base between E122Q-opsin and chromophore.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Chromophore-exchange experiments in live cells have previously been done only in salamander red cones.
source: Chromophore-exchange experiments in live cells have previously been done only in salamander red cones (Kefalov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kefalov et al., 2005.

claim: After dark incubation with 9-cis-retinal for 3 hr, the absorption spectra of dark-adapted zebrafish LWS, MWS and SWS cones all shifted to shorter wavelengths.
source: After dark incubation with 15 µM 9-cis-retinal for 3 hr, the absorption spectra of dark-adapted, native (11-cis) LWS, MWS and SWS cones all shifted to shorter wavelengths, indicating incorporation of 9-cis-retinal (Figure 3B, with native spectra shown in black and spectra after 3 hr incubation with 15 µM 9-cis-retinal shown in red).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The spectral shift due to dark chromophore-exchange was too small to be resolved for zebrafish UVS cones.
source: Because pigments with shorter λmax's show smaller λmax-differences between their 11-cis- and 9-cis-conjugated forms (the latter obtained by a full bleach followed by dark incubation with 9-cis; indicated in green in Figure 3B), the absolute amount of spectral shift due to dark chromophore-exchange was smaller for MWS and SWS cones than for LWS cones and was too small to be resolved for UVS cones.
evidence: This is an observation from the spectral measurements in the current study.

claim: The time constant of dark chromophore-exchange for zebrafish LWS cones is 37 min at 20–22°C.
source: A single-exponential fit to the collected data (mean ± SD, 20–22°C) gives a time constant of 37 min, ~4 fold faster than previously found for salamander red cones (Kefalov et al., 2005), although the exchange in zebrafish did not appear to have reached completion (i.e.,<100%, see Figure 3C), possibly because of some 11-cis-retinal released from the pigment staying around and competing with the exogenous 9-cis-retinal.
evidence: This is calculated from the time course data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The time constant of dark chromophore-exchange for zebrafish LWS cones is ~4 fold faster than previously found for salamander red cones.
source: A single-exponential fit to the collected data (mean ± SD, 20–22°C) gives a time constant of 37 min, ~4 fold faster than previously found for salamander red cones (Kefalov et al., 2005), although the exchange in zebrafish did not appear to have reached completion (i.e.,<100%, see Figure 3C), possibly because of some 11-cis-retinal released from the pigment staying around and competing with the exogenous 9-cis-retinal.
evidence: This is a comparison with the value from Kefalov et al., 2005.

claim: The chromophore-exchange in zebrafish LWS cones did not appear to have reached completion.
source: A single-exponential fit to the collected data (mean ± SD, 20–22°C) gives a time constant of 37 min, ~4 fold faster than previously found for salamander red cones (Kefalov et al., 2005), although the exchange in zebrafish did not appear to have reached completion (i.e.,<100%, see Figure 3C), possibly because of some 11-cis-retinal released from the pigment staying around and competing with the exogenous 9-cis-retinal.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The incomplete chromophore-exchange in zebrafish LWS cones is possibly because some 11-cis-retinal released from the pigment stays around and competes with the exogenous 9-cis-retinal.
source: A single-exponential fit to the collected data (mean ± SD, 20–22°C) gives a time constant of 37 min, ~4 fold faster than previously found for salamander red cones (Kefalov et al., 2005), although the exchange in zebrafish did not appear to have reached completion (i.e.,<100%, see Figure 3C), possibly because of some 11-cis-retinal released from the pigment staying around and competing with the exogenous 9-cis-retinal.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of incomplete exchange.

claim: Dark chromophore-exchange for zebrafish MWS and SWS cones appears to be faster than for LWS cones, with significant shift occurring within the first 10 min of dark incubation.
source: The time courses of dark chromophore-exchange for other zebrafish cone pigments were not well-resolved owing to the smaller spectral shift, but appeared to be faster at least for MWS and SWS cones, in that we found a significant shift to have occurred within the first 10 min of dark incubation (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: Zebrafish rhodopsin shows no obvious dark chromophore-exchange even after incubation with 9-cis-retinal for 6 hr.
source: In contrast, zebrafish rhodopsin showed no obvious dark chromophore-exchange even after incubation with 9-cis-retinal for 6 hr (blue trace in Figure 3B, rod panel), same as mouse rhodopsin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dark chromophore-exchange appears to be a general property for cone pigments with a time constant of the order of an hour.
source: Thus, at least for salamander and zebrafish, dark chromophore-exchange appears to be a general property for cone pigments with a time constant of the order of an hour, whereas rhodopsins behave quite differently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measurements from salamander and zebrafish cone pigments.

claim: Rhodopsins behave quite differently from cone pigments with respect to dark chromophore-exchange.
source: Thus, at least for salamander and zebrafish, dark chromophore-exchange appears to be a general property for cone pigments with a time constant of the order of an hour, whereas rhodopsins behave quite differently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measurements from the current study.

claim: Rhodopsin purified from bovine rod outer segments dissociates into opsin and 11-cis-retinal in darkness, with a half life for holo-rhodopsin of the order of days.
source: A paper just appeared (Tian et al., 2017)﻿ reporting that rhodopsin purified from bovine rod outer segments dissociates into opsin and 11-cis-retinal in darkness, with a half life for holo-rhodopsin of the order of days.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tian et al., 2017.

claim: The rhodopsin dissociation behavior reported by Tian et al. is not incompatible with the findings in this study because it is very different in time scale from the chromophore exchange in cone pigments.
source: This rhodopsin behavior is not incompatible with our findings here because it is clearly still very different in time scale from the chromophore exchange in cone pigments, which occurs within hours.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the time scales of different processes.

claim: The λmax of dark-adapted RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods is 499.9 ± 4.8 nm.
source: For RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods, λmax's are (A) 499.9 ± 4.8 nm (n = 33 recordings), (B) 495.6 ± 3.0 nm (n = 5 recordings, p=0.06), (C) 501.3 ± 4.5 nm (n = 6 recordings, p=0.52) and (D) 481.6 ± 4.1 nm (n = 5 recordings, p<0.0001), with p values from Student's t-test comparing with (A).
evidence: This is measured by microspectrophotometry and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The λmax of dark-adapted RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods is 480.9 ± 5.4 nm.
source: For RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods, λmax's are (A) 480.9 ± 5.4 nm (n = 7 recordings), (B) 479.6 ± 3.6 nm (n = 5 recordings, p=0.65), (C) 479.2 ± 3.9 nm (n = 5 recordings, p=0.56) and (D) 469.3 ± 3.2 nm (n = 8 recordings, p=0.0002), with p values from Student's t-test comparing with (A).
evidence: This is measured by microspectrophotometry and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effective collecting area (Ae) for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods is 0.44 ± 0.09 µm².
source: As such, we found Ae to be 0.44 ± 0.09 µm2 (mean ± SD, n = 10) for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods and 0.35 ± 0.10 µm2 (mean ± SD, n = 18) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods.
evidence: This is measured from electrophysiological experiments in the current study.

claim: The effective collecting area (Ae) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods is 0.35 ± 0.10 µm².
source: As such, we found Ae to be 0.44 ± 0.09 µm2 (mean ± SD, n = 10) for RhoWT/WT;Gcaps-/- rods and 0.35 ± 0.10 µm2 (mean ± SD, n = 18) for RhoE122Q/E122Q;Gcaps-/- rods.
evidence: This is measured from electrophysiological experiments in the current study.

claim: The E122Q/WT pigment-content ratio based on effective collecting area is 1/1.26.
